title: THE BIBLE SAID IT. BUT DID GOD MEAN WHAT YOU THINK HE MEANT?
paragraphs: THE BIBLE SAID IT. BUT DID GOD MEAN WHAT YOU THINK HE MEANT?
The Dangerous Mistake of Reading Scripture Without Context—and the Life-Changing Truth About What Jesus Actually Calls Us to Obey

What if I told you that you could read the Bible every morning, underline your favorite verses, memorize entire chapters, defend Christianity in arguments… and still misunderstand what God was actually saying?
Not because you hated His Word.
Not because you wanted to rebel.
But because nobody ever taught you the difference between reading a biblical command and understanding it.
And what if the very verse you've been using to condemn someone was never meant to be used that way?
Or worse…
What if the verse you've been using to excuse your own behavior actually demands repentance?
This is where things become uncomfortable.
Because the question isn't simply whether Christians should take the Bible literally.
The deeper question is whether we love God's Word enough to let it correct our assumptions—even when those assumptions have been wrapped in religion for years.

And somewhere between the ancient world of Scripture and the modern world we inhabit, an enormous number of people have confused being faithful to the Bible with being faithful to their own interpretation of it.
Those are not always the same thing.
Imagine a young woman sitting alone after church.
She's been told that because 1 Corinthians 11 speaks about women covering their heads, she is dishonoring God whenever she prays without a covering.
She wants to obey Jesus. She genuinely does.

But nobody has explained the cultural meaning of head coverings in Corinth, the argument Paul was making about honor and worship, or why faithful Christians disagree about the command's application today.
So she lives with guilt.
Now imagine a man sitting three rows behind her.
He has read Jesus' command to love his enemies.
He knows exactly what it means.
But he refuses to forgive the brother who betrayed him.
He has explanations. He has justifications. He has a whole history of being hurt.
And somehow, the woman is terrified of disobeying a command whose modern application requires careful interpretation, while the man comfortably ignores a command Jesus made unmistakably clear.
Do you see the tragedy?
We can become obsessed with the commands we haven't understood while negotiating our way around the commands we understand perfectly.
And Jesus did not call us to become experts at religious appearances.
He called us to follow Him.
There is a sentence from Scripture that should make every serious Bible reader tremble—not with hopeless fear, but with holy humility.
In 2 Timothy 2:15, Paul urges Timothy to handle the word of truth correctly.
The Greek expression is:
ὀρθοτομοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας
orthotomounta ton logon tēs alētheias
A careful rendering is “rightly handling the word of truth.”
The verb orthotomeō carries the basic sense of cutting straight. In this context, it describes handling or teaching God's truth correctly.
Paul is not inviting Timothy to manipulate Scripture until it agrees with his preferences.
He is calling him to deal faithfully with what God has actually revealed.
Because you can quote the right words and still reach the wrong conclusion.
You can repeat a command accurately and still misapply it.
You can hold a Bible in your hands while refusing to hear the voice of the God who gave it.
And sometimes the most dangerous misunderstanding isn't caused by someone rejecting Scripture.
It's caused by someone being absolutely certain they could never misunderstand it.
Consider a command from the Old Testament that most Christians do not practice today.
Leviticus 19:19 forbids wearing a garment made of two kinds of material.
If every biblical command must be applied directly and identically to every believer in every century, what happens when you open your wardrobe?
But here's where the discussion gets more serious.
Just a few verses earlier, Leviticus 19:18 commands God's people to love their neighbors as themselves.
Jesus later identifies this command as one of the greatest commandments.
So why does the Christian church continue to affirm the command to love one's neighbor while generally not treating the prohibition concerning mixed fabrics as binding?
Did Christians simply choose the verses they liked?
That would be a fair accusation if there were no biblical explanation.
But there is.
And it begins with understanding that the Bible is not a random collection of isolated instructions.

It tells one unfolding story of creation, human rebellion, God's covenant promises, Israel's calling, the coming of Jesus Christ, His death and resurrection, and the formation of a redeemed people through the Holy Spirit.
The commandments within that story must be understood according to whom God addressed, why He gave them, what covenant governed them, and how they relate to the finished work of Christ.
God's Word does not change into something meaningless when its historical setting is understood.
Its meaning becomes clearer.
When God gave Israel the Law through Moses, He was speaking to a particular covenant people within a particular historical relationship.
That Law included commands concerning sacrifices, priesthood, ritual purity, food, festivals, social justice, sexual morality, and the worship of the living God.
These commands were not meaningless.
They revealed God's holiness, distinguished Israel as His covenant people, regulated life in that community, and pointed forward in various ways to His redemptive purposes.
But then Jesus came.
And the arrival of Jesus changed everything about how God's people relate to the Mosaic covenant.
In Matthew 5:17, Jesus declares that He came not to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them.
The Greek verb is:
πληρῶσαι
plērōsai — “to fulfill.”
This does not mean that Jesus came to declare the Old Testament worthless.
It means His life and mission bring God's earlier revelation toward its intended fulfillment.
That is why the New Testament describes Jesus as our great High Priest and His sacrifice as sufficient in a way the repeated animal sacrifices could never be.
Hebrews 10 explains that the sacrifices of the old covenant could not finally remove sins, but Christ offered Himself once for all.
Think about what that means.
A Christian does not offer an animal sacrifice for forgiveness today, not because God's holiness has become less important, but because Jesus has accomplished what those sacrifices anticipated.
We don't need another lamb on the altar.
The Lamb of God has come.
We don't need to pretend that Calvary never happened in order to prove that we respect Moses.
The cross is not an interruption of God's story.
It is central to its fulfillment.
And when we forget that, we risk reading the Bible as though Jesus never came.
But be careful.
Because there is an equally dangerous mistake on the other side.
Some people hear the word “context” and treat it like permission to escape anything Scripture says that makes them uncomfortable.
They say adultery was condemned because ancient societies were different.
They say sexual purity was only important because of cultural expectations.
They say forgiveness, generosity, humility, repentance, and holiness must all be reconsidered because modern life is complicated.
And suddenly, historical context stops being a tool for understanding God's Word.
It becomes a weapon for silencing it.
That is not faithful interpretation.
That is selective obedience wearing academic clothing.
The same Jesus who fulfilled the Law also called people to repent.
The same Jesus who welcomed sinners also told them to leave their lives of sin.
The same Jesus who condemned religious hypocrisy also taught that loving Him is inseparable from keeping His commandments.
In John 14:15, Jesus says:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.” (KJV)
In Greek:
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.
Ean agapate me, tas entolas tas emas tērēsete.
The sense is, “If you love me, you will keep my commandments.”
The Greek wording presents obedience as the response flowing from love for Christ.
Not a performance to purchase salvation.
Not a religious transaction to make God indebted to us.
But the fruit of a heart that has encountered the Savior.
Grace does not mean Jesus has no authority over your life.
Grace means the One who has authority over your life loved you enough to die for you.
And that changes how we read everything.
Now consider one of the most frequently quoted commands in the Bible.
“Judge not, that ye be not judged.” (Matthew 7:1, KJV)
How many times have you heard that verse used to silence any discussion about sin?
Someone confronts dishonesty.
“Don't judge.”
Someone lovingly warns a friend about destructive behavior.
“Don't judge.”
Someone calls believers to repentance.
“Who are you to judge me?”
But read the surrounding passage.
Jesus condemns hypocritical judgment. He describes someone trying to remove a speck from another person's eye while ignoring a beam in his own.
Then He tells that person to remove the beam first so that he can see clearly enough to help his brother.
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say the speck should remain forever.
He says the hypocrite must first confront his own sin.
The passage is not permission to abandon moral discernment.
It is a command to practice discernment without hypocrisy.
Context doesn't weaken Jesus' words.
It makes them more searching.
Because suddenly, the question isn't merely whether you have the right to correct somebody.
The question is whether you've allowed God to correct you first.
And that hurts.
Especially when you've spent years using truth as a weapon against other people while refusing to let it become a mirror for your own soul.
Now think about another passage.
In 1 Timothy 2:9, Paul instructs women concerning modest dress, mentioning braided hair, gold, pearls, and expensive clothing.
Some readers conclude that every form of braided hair or jewelry must be sinful.
Others dismiss the entire passage as irrelevant ancient culture.
But the surrounding argument concerns godliness, modesty, and good works rather than outward displays of wealth or status.
The historical setting helps us understand why these particular expressions of adornment mattered.
Yet the underlying concern remains deeply relevant.
Are we using appearance to display status, attract admiration, or make ourselves the center of attention?
Does the way we present ourselves reflect humility and reverence toward God?
Christians may differ over the precise application of particular clothing instructions, but they should not dismiss the moral concerns Paul is addressing.
And this is where mature biblical interpretation requires something many of us don't enjoy.
Patience.
Humility.
A willingness to say, “I need to study this more carefully.”
Not every passage is equally difficult.
Not every Christian disagreement has equal biblical support.
And not every interpretation becomes valid simply because someone sincerely believes it.
But sincere believers can disagree about difficult applications while remaining united in the authority of Scripture and the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Romans 14 gives us a powerful example.
Paul addresses disputes concerning food and the observance of particular days.

Rather than treating every difference as proof of rebellion, he calls believers to act in faith, honor the Lord, avoid despising one another, and refrain from placing unnecessary stumbling blocks in another believer's path.
That is not moral relativism.
It is spiritually mature discernment.
The same Paul who allows differences over certain disputed practices also speaks firmly against sexual immorality, idolatry, greed, and other sins.
So we cannot use Romans 14 to make every biblical command optional.
We must distinguish between matters Scripture directly identifies as sinful and matters where faithful Christians may reach different conclusions about application.
And we must do it with an open Bible, not merely an open opinion.
There's another example that might surprise you.
When Jesus tells His disciples in Matthew 5:29 that if their right eye causes them to sin, they should tear it out, are Christians supposed to physically mutilate themselves?
No.
Jesus is using deliberately shocking language to communicate the deadly seriousness of sin.
The immediate context concerns lust and the need for decisive repentance.
A literalistic reading that ignores Jesus' rhetorical language can distort His meaning.
But a contextual reading does not make His warning harmless.
It makes the warning impossible to escape.
Jesus is saying that sin must not be treated casually.
Whatever draws you toward destruction must be confronted with seriousness.
Not by harming your body, but by turning away from sin and removing opportunities that nourish it.
And suddenly the passage becomes painfully personal.
That secret conversation you keep returning to.
That bitterness you've been feeding for years.
That habit you've renamed a weakness because you don't want to call it disobedience.
That relationship you know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
You may not need to remove your eye.
But you may need to remove an app.
You may need to end a conversation.
You may need to confess something.
You may need to stop pretending that because nobody knows, God doesn't see.
Context has not given you an escape route.
It has brought you face-to-face with the actual demand of Jesus.
And perhaps that is why some people resist careful Bible study.
Not because context makes Scripture less demanding.
But because understanding Scripture accurately can make its demands much harder to evade.
Yet there is something even more beautiful beneath all of this.
The Bible was never given merely to produce people who win arguments about the Bible.
It was given to reveal God, make us wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and equip us for every good work.
That's Paul's teaching in 2 Timothy 3:15–17.
Scripture is not simply a collection of rules waiting to be extracted from their setting.
It is God's inspired Word, bearing witness to His redemptive purposes and directing us to the Savior.
And if our interpretation makes us more arrogant, more cruel, more self-righteous, and less like Jesus, we need to examine whether we have truly understood what we read.
That does not mean truth must always feel comfortable.
Sometimes the truth will confront you.
Sometimes it will expose your pride.
Sometimes it will tell you that what you've been calling love is actually compromise.
Sometimes it will tell you that what you've been calling holiness is actually contempt.
And sometimes it will reveal that you've been defending a religious tradition more passionately than you've been following Christ.
Remember the religious leaders who challenged Jesus.
Many of them knew the Scriptures extraordinarily well.
They could debate details of the Law.
They guarded traditions.
They were deeply invested in religious correctness.
Yet in John 5:39–40, Jesus confronts people who searched the Scriptures while refusing to come to Him for life.
Imagine that.
Studying the words that testify about the Messiah while rejecting the Messiah standing in front of them.
That is one of the most heartbreaking warnings in the Gospels.
You can become so attached to your interpretation that you stop listening to the One Scripture is revealing.
You can know the vocabulary of holiness without having a humble heart.
You can defend the truth without walking in the truth.
And you can spend years trying to prove you're right while Jesus is calling you to surrender.
This is why understanding historical context matters.
When we read an ancient letter, we should remember that it was written to real people facing real circumstances.
When Paul writes to the Corinthians, he is not composing random inspirational sayings for social media.
He is addressing an actual church struggling with divisions, sexual immorality, lawsuits, worship disorders, spiritual gifts, and confusion about the resurrection.
When we read the prophets, we should ask what covenant unfaithfulness, injustice, idolatry, or hope they were addressing.
When we read the Psalms, we should recognize poetry, lament, worship, and imagery.
When we read Proverbs, we should recognize wisdom sayings that generally describe how life works, rather than treating every proverb as an unconditional promise.
When we read Revelation, we must take seriously its apocalyptic imagery, its first-century recipients, its Old Testament echoes, and its ultimate testimony to the victory of Jesus Christ.
Different biblical genres communicate truth in different ways.
A parable is not interpreted exactly like a legal command.
A vision is not read exactly like a historical narrative.
A proverb is not handled exactly like a covenant promise.
Taking the Bible seriously means respecting the way God chose to communicate.
And here is something worth remembering whenever someone insists that “literal” is always the same as “faithful.”
Jesus says in John 10:9, “I am the door.”
Christians do not believe Jesus is a wooden panel with hinges.
We understand that He is using metaphor to communicate the truth that He is the way of salvation and entrance into the security of His flock.
Recognizing figurative language does not mean rejecting the truth of His statement.
It means understanding it.
The goal is not to make every sentence literal in the same wooden sense.
The goal is to understand the meaning intended by the biblical text and respond faithfully to it.

That means paying attention to the words, the grammar, the literary form, the surrounding passage, the historical setting, the place of the passage within the whole Bible, and above all, its relationship to God's revelation in Jesus Christ.
But it also means something more intimate.
It means approaching Scripture with a teachable heart.
Because you are not simply studying an ancient document.
You are encountering the written Word of the living God.
And His Word is not something we stand above as judges.
It is something under which we stand as disciples.
There is a beautiful Hebrew expression in Psalm 119:105:
נֵר־לְרַגְלִי דְבָרֶךָ וְאוֹר לִנְתִיבָתִי
Ner-leragli devarekha ve'or lintivati.
“Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.” (KJV)
Notice the image.
A lamp for your feet.
A light for your path.
Not a weapon for humiliating people who are struggling.
Not a decoration to prove that you are religious.
Not a collection of disconnected slogans to justify whatever you already wanted to believe.
A lamp.
A light.
Something that helps you walk.
And walking implies movement.
Growth.
Correction.
Direction.
Sometimes the light exposes danger ahead.
Sometimes it reveals the dirt on your own feet.
Sometimes it shows you that the road you were confidently traveling was leading away from the heart of God.
But the purpose of the light is not to destroy the person who needs guidance.
It is to lead that person into truth.
This is why the question “Should Christians take every biblical command literally?” cannot be answered responsibly with a simple yes or no.
We must take every biblical command seriously.
We must believe that Scripture speaks truthfully and authoritatively according to what it actually teaches.

But we must not assume that every command was addressed directly to every person in every age, or that every expression should be understood without regard for its genre, covenant setting, and historical circumstances.
Some commands express enduring moral obligations.
Some belong specifically to Israel's covenant life under Moses.
Some were directed to particular people in particular situations.
Some are fulfilled through the person and work of Christ.
Some require careful discernment to apply their enduring principles faithfully in a different cultural setting.
And sometimes Christians disagree about which category best explains a particular passage.
The answer is not to abandon Scripture.
The answer is to study it more faithfully.
Acts 15 provides a remarkable example.
The early church faced a deeply consequential question: Must Gentile believers be circumcised and required to keep the Mosaic Law in order to be saved?
This was not a minor disagreement over personal preference.
It concerned the nature of salvation and the identity of God's people.

The apostles and elders examined what God had done among the Gentiles, considered the testimony of Scripture, and concluded that Gentile believers should not be placed under the Mosaic Law as a requirement for salvation.
Peter's testimony pointed to salvation through the grace of the Lord Jesus.
Think about the significance.
The early church did not resolve the issue by pretending the Old Testament did not exist.
Nor did it simply impose every Israelite covenant requirement upon Gentile Christians.
It interpreted God's earlier revelation in light of what He had accomplished through Jesus Christ.
That is not a modern excuse for disobedience.
It is part of the New Testament's own witness.
And perhaps now the question is becoming clearer.
The issue isn't whether we should choose between biblical obedience and historical context.
Faithful obedience requires understanding what Scripture actually means.
Without context, we can impose burdens God has not placed upon people.
Without obedience, we can turn careful study into an excuse for refusing the Lord who speaks.
Both errors wound the church.
Both distort the Gospel.
Both can leave people spiritually exhausted.
Maybe you've experienced that exhaustion yourself.
Maybe you grew up in a home where every question was treated like rebellion.
You were told what the Bible meant, but rarely shown why.
You learned to be afraid of getting a verse wrong.
You learned that asking questions might make people doubt your faith.
And eventually, you stopped asking.
Or perhaps your story is the opposite.
Maybe you've spent years around people who explained away nearly every difficult command.
Every call to holiness became “cultural.”
Every warning about sin became “outdated.”
Every demand for surrender became “someone else's interpretation.”
And eventually, the Bible stopped correcting anybody.
It only confirmed what everyone already wanted to believe.
Both experiences can leave a person spiritually hungry.
One is burdened by human rules.
The other is starved of divine truth.
But Jesus offers something better than either extreme.
He calls us to truth and grace.
To repentance and forgiveness.
To reverence and understanding.
To conviction without despair.
To freedom without rebellion.
And this is where the Gospel becomes so much more than a debate about interpretation.
Because when we finally understand what Scripture says about human sin, we discover something that should silence every self-righteous heart.
None of us has obeyed God perfectly.
Not the scholar who understands biblical Greek.
Not the pastor who can explain the Mosaic covenant.
Not the Christian who has memorized a hundred passages.
Not the person who proudly declares, “I just believe what the Bible says.”
We have all sinned and fall short of the glory of God, as Romans 3:23 teaches.
And no amount of interpretive accuracy can erase our guilt.
Correct theology cannot serve as our atoning sacrifice.
Religious knowledge cannot raise us from spiritual death.
We do not save ourselves by becoming better Bible readers.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the Jesus who saves us also teaches us how to live.
That is why Ephesians 2:8–10 holds together what we so often tear apart.
Salvation is God's gift, not the result of works.
Yet those who are saved are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is the root.
Obedience is the fruit.
Never confuse the two.
If you make obedience the price of God's love, you distort the Gospel.
If you use God's love as permission to remain unrepentant, you also distort the Gospel.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could earn salvation by following rules.
And He did not shed His blood so we could celebrate sin without repentance.
He came to rescue sinners and transform lives.
That includes yours.
That includes mine.
And it includes the person you have been so eager to correct.
Perhaps the most important question you can ask when opening Scripture is not simply, “How can I use this verse?”
It is, “Lord, what are You teaching through this passage, and how should I respond faithfully?”
Before claiming a promise, understand its setting.
Before applying a command, identify its original audience and purpose.
Before condemning someone, examine the passage and your own heart.
Before dismissing a difficult teaching, ask whether your discomfort comes from a genuine interpretive problem or from resistance to obedience.
And before turning your interpretation into a test of everyone else's faithfulness, remember how much you still have to learn.
The Holy Spirit does not call us to intellectual laziness.
He calls us to love God with our hearts, souls, and minds.
Study is not the enemy of devotion.
Careful interpretation is not the enemy of faith.
And humility is not the enemy of conviction.
You can be deeply committed to biblical authority while admitting that your understanding of a particular passage may need correction.
In fact, that humility may be one of the clearest signs that you take biblical authority seriously.
Because if Scripture truly has authority over you, then you must be willing to change when Scripture shows that you were wrong.
Not merely when a preacher agrees with you.
Not merely when a favorite teacher confirms your position.
Not merely when a verse can be made to support what you've always believed.
But when the Word of God, rightly understood, confronts you.
And that may be the hardest form of obedience.
Not following a rule that makes you feel religious.
But surrendering an interpretation that makes you feel superior.
Not winning an argument.
But confessing a sin.
Not proving that someone else is wrong.
But allowing Jesus to change what is wrong within you.
Somewhere today, there is a believer carrying unnecessary guilt because someone applied a biblical passage without understanding its context.
Somewhere else, there is a believer living in unnecessary compromise because someone convinced them that historical context makes holiness optional.
Both need the same thing.
Not another human opinion dressed in biblical language.
They need the truth of God's Word, understood faithfully, proclaimed graciously, and centered on Jesus Christ.
And maybe you needed this reminder too.
Maybe you've been wounded by someone who quoted Scripture without love.
Maybe you've used Scripture to wound someone else.
Maybe you've avoided certain passages because you're afraid of what they might require.
Maybe you've been defending your position so fiercely that you've forgotten the purpose of discipleship is becoming more like Christ.
If this article has exposed something in your heart, don't rush past it.
Pray about it.
Open the Scriptures again.
Ask God for wisdom.
Seek counsel from mature believers who handle the Bible carefully and live under its authority.
And remember that repentance is not the end of your story.
In Christ, repentance can be the beginning of restoration.
That's what makes the Gospel so extraordinary.
Jesus does not wait for you to become a perfect theologian before offering you grace.
He calls you to come to Him.
He does not excuse your sin.
He offers forgiveness.
He does not affirm every religious assumption you've inherited.
He invites you into truth.
He does not merely repair your reputation.
He begins transforming your heart.
And whether your story has been marked by legalism, confusion, compromise, shame, or spiritual pride, the invitation remains.
Come to Jesus.
The Savior who forgave sinners still forgives sinners.
The Lord who confronted hypocrisy still confronts hypocrisy.
The Christ who fulfilled the Scriptures still calls His people to hear His Word and follow Him.
Your past misunderstandings do not have to define your future obedience.
Your past rebellion does not have to be the final chapter.
Your religious failures do not have to be the end of your story.
Because the heart of Christianity is not a person successfully climbing toward God through flawless rule-keeping.
It is God coming to rescue sinners through Jesus Christ.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From spiritual confusion to the light of truth.
From self-righteousness to humility.
From rebellion to repentance.
From death to life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Have you ever discovered that a Bible verse you had believed or used for years meant something different when you finally studied its context?
Or have you ever been hurt by someone who used Scripture without understanding it?
Not as a performance for other people.
But as a sincere expression of your desire to be corrected, shaped, and transformed by God's Word.
Perhaps this community can become a place where we open our Bibles together rather than simply argue about them.
And if this message helped you understand something you've struggled with, please don't let it disappear into your feed.
Return to it when you encounter a difficult passage.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to win a debate.
But to encourage a deeper love for God's truth.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, difficult questions are welcomed, sin is not disguised, grace is not cheapened, and Jesus Christ remains at the center.
Because discipleship does not end when an article ends.
It continues when the Bible is opened again tomorrow.
When a difficult conversation is approached with humility.
When a hidden sin is confessed.
When someone chooses forgiveness instead of revenge.
When a wounded believer discovers that God's Word, properly understood, is not an instrument of cruelty but a revelation of His holy and gracious character.
We believe this work is worth supporting, not because any ministry can replace the local church, but because biblical truth deserves to be shared carefully, faithfully, and generously.
If God has used this ministry to encourage you, teach you, or draw you closer to Christ, prayerfully consider helping us reach more people.
God loves a cheerful giver, as 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches.
So we do not want you to give out of guilt.
We invite you to give from conviction, gratitude, and a genuine desire to help make Christ known.
These free resources are part of our desire to help make biblical learning and spiritual encouragement accessible to more people.
Pray for this ministry.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Help someone open the Bible with fresh eyes.
And most importantly, live what you are learning.
Because our deepest hope is not that people will simply recognize the name Gospel Warrior.
It is that they will come to know, love, trust, and follow Jesus Christ.
One day, nobody will be impressed by how many biblical arguments we won if we never learned to love the God whose Word we defended.
And nobody will enter the kingdom of God because they mastered religious appearances.
Our hope is Christ.
Our righteousness is found in Christ.
Our salvation is through Christ.
And our obedience is the grateful response of people who have been redeemed by Christ.
So yes, study the history.
Learn the context.
Pay attention to the original languages.
Read carefully.
Ask difficult questions.
Test interpretations against the whole counsel of Scripture.
But never allow your knowledge about the Bible to replace your relationship with the Savior to whom the Bible bears witness.
Because the goal was never to become someone who can quote every command while remaining unchanged.
The goal is to become someone whose life increasingly reflects the Lord who gave His life to save us.
And when the final page of your earthly story is written, may it not merely say that you knew the Scriptures.
May it say that through the grace of God, you came to know the Savior, trusted His Gospel, loved His truth, and followed Him.
The greatest tragedy is not opening the Bible and discovering you were wrong. It is closing the Bible unchanged because you were too proud to be corrected.
